Why do you think people get so worked up over "best of" lists?

Whether the list consists of artists, albums, or songs; or whether the time frame is all-time, a particular decade, or the current year, one thing that's certain is that the list is going to create controversy.  That's probably the main reason why media outlets continue to pump them out.  The negative comments about these lists usually fit within one of several categories (for each category I'll just mention albums, but it also applies to artists and songs).  There's the complaint that this album is ranked too high or too low either in isolation or in relation to another album on the list.  There's the complaint that this album sucks and that it shouldn't be on the list at all.  And, of course, there's the complaint that "you forgot album x," as if it's brilliance should be so obvious to everybody that the listmaker(s) couldn't have possibly omitted the album due to reasons of taste or quality.

In some ways all of this is natural, and depending on the tone it can even be fun to discuss.  However, it's the intensity and the vitriol of some of the reactions that has always seemed absurd to me.  It's a list put together by strangers with opinions.  Even if they're professional critics, they're not all knowing arbiters of what's good and you definitely don't have to listen to them.  I certainly don't a lot of the time.  On the other hand, they're also not idiots who don't know anything about music.  A list is useful to me if it introduces me to music I haven't heard before or it reminds me of stuff I haven't heard in a while.  The rankings and inclusions/omissions don't interest me too much.  In regard to the people that do care about those things to an intense degree, why do you think that is?  Do people need their taste validated?  Are they in such a bubble that they can't handle differing opinions?  Do you think there is something in all of this that's specific to music, or is it the same explanation for why people get upset over lists related to movies, sports, etc.?

Sophisti-pop, and other genres that have never had a revival

One of my favorite musical discoveries in the last decade was Sophisti-pop. While the name is a bit, frankly, not great, the genre itself is absolutely stacked full of critically acclaimed artists and albums. Artists like China Crisis, Roxy Music, Prefab Sprout, Everything but the Girl's early work, Level 42, and my personal favorite, The Blue Nile. It's a very specific sound, and it emerged at a very specific point in time. It got moderately to very popular, depending on the artist (Sade was massive, for instance), but for all intents and purposes only practically existed between 1982 or 83 to around 1990, and fizzled back into the underground after.

While other artists have played with this sound on songs here and there, like Blood Orange and Carly Rae Jepsen, it's never had a true revival at any point in time. 

So that got me thinking: What other notable 20^(th) century styles of music have never had a popular revival, even for a short period of time? Obviously, this isn't focused on a song or two that might have come out, but proper revivals, such as the swing and rockabilly revival in the mid 90's, or the disco and funk revival that happened at the end of the 2010's into the early 2020's.

Copyright for lyrics is weird

I’ve always found the idea of copyrighting song lyrics a little strange. I completely understand why the song itself and the songwriter’s work need to be protected, but lyrics are literally written to be heard and repeated. The artist sings those exact words publicly, millions of people hear them, sing along, memorize them, and even discuss them. So it feels a bit odd that simply writing down the same words we just heard can suddenly become a copyright issue. I’m not arguing that artists shouldn’t own their work or be compensated for it. I just think there’s something inherently funny about the fact that you can freely hear, sing, and remember the words, but reproducing those same words in text is treated differently.

Does anyone believe that poptimism has had a negative effect on music discourse?

This question has been on my mind a lot lately. In my opinion I feel like poptimism has had a detrimental impact on music criticism. Poptimism from what I can understand correct me If I'm mistaken, attempted to contextualize and view pop music with more rigour. It was also done with the goal of trying to uplift forms of pop music by marginalized communities. 

Although I agree with the broader goal of wanting to give more recognition to musicians from marginalized communities, In my opinion I believe the broader idea of treating pop music with the same rigour as other genres of music is misguided and short sided.

 In my opinion, I feel like poptimism has created an environment in which some of the most wealthy, privileged artists have been able to brand themselves as underdogs. I find it to be ridiculous. 

These pop musicians are making some of the most commercialized,sterile and accessible music out there. In my opinion, I just don't believe treating a music genre(where one of the main mo's is to make as much profit as possible is valid in my opinion. 

That's not to say that Rock,Country,Hip hop,Jazz, Electronic music etc are devoid from the interests of capitalism and commodification. I do believe it becomes more aggrandized with pop music insofar as it becomes more acceptable to engage in hagiographic praise of these multi millionaire and in a few cases billionaires musicians accumulating and hoarding as much wealth as possible. On a related note, I find the idea of poptimism being a voice for marginalized communities questionable. Why have we allowed pop music to be a stand in for these communities. Folks from marginalized communities are making great music in a myriad of genres.

Is the idea of a difficult album still relevant?

I was listening to something really abrasive the other day and remembered how people used to talk about certain albums as being 'difficult' or 'an acquired taste'. Like you had to really work to appreciate them. Think early Swans or some avant-garde jazz.

  
But in the age of instant streaming and endless playlists do we still engage with music that way? It feels like if something doesn't grab you in the first 30 seconds people just skip it. There's so much out there that if you're not immediately hooked it's easy to just move on.

  
Are there still albums that demand multiple listens to truly 'get'? Or has the way we consume music made that kind of experience less common? I wonder if newer artists even aim for that kind of slow burn anymore. Is it even a viable strategy to make music that isn't instantly digestible when attention spans are so short? What are your thoughts?

Why was it "cool" to hate popular music in the 2000s and early 2010s but it's kinda lame now?

When I was a kid this attitude against modern music was a lot more common. I remember in the early 2010s tons of "CLASSIC ROCK IS THE ONLY REAL MUSIC, TODAY'S MUSIC SUCKS".

But now this attitude still exists... but not only is it not nearly as common as it used to be, it also feels rather...corny.

In the 2000s, a lot of people thought 80s music was better than the music at the time. In the 2010s a lot of people thought 90s music was better than the music at the time. You used to constantly hear people say "today's music sucks, I miss Nirvana, Guns N Roses, etc."... You've seen the memes.

But something feels different now. I've noticed that today’s mainstream music (2020s) doesn’t seem to get roasted as harshly as it used to be.

It seems the 2020s have reverted that 20 year cycle and nowadays a LOT of people (not everybody) seem to think that today's popular music is better than it was in the 2000s and early 10s (first few years of the 2010s). Not everyone thinks this but it's interesting to note... so many people say "today's music is better". You NEVER heard that phrase in the 2000s or early 2010s.

  
Am I the only one who's noticed this?

What do you think. Do you think we've leard to live and let live, or do you think today's music is just better than what we grew up with? Or maybe we've just stopped getting irrationally angry at what teenage girls like?

Why do albums get the wrong genre assigned to them?

I’m listening to Fleetwood Mac’s In Chicago right now and it is literally blues. Yet it’s classed as Rock, and it got me thinking about how genres actually get assigned to albums.

For context, I’m still very new to rock. This is actually my first year properly listening to the genre. I’ve already made several rock playlists, and one thing I’ve quickly realised is just how massive it is. It’s commercially huge, incredibly popular, ridiculously broad, and filled with so many different sounds that I’m still discovering where everything fits.

I’m liking rock in ways I genuinely didn’t expect, and it keeps surprising me. At this point I wouldn’t even be surprised if Rock appears for the first time among my most listened genres in my ’26Replay. Probably somewhere near the bottom because I only really started getting into it this year, but still.

And maybe being new to it is partly why the genre labels stand out to me so much.

Fleetwood Mac has been one of the more interesting bands to discover because the further I go through their music, the more I notice how much the sound changes. Early on, a lot of what I’m hearing feels overwhelmingly rooted in blues. Then, as I move further through their albums, I start noticing more and more rock coming into it, until the balance feels completely different.

And then later on it almost feels like they end up somewhere much more polished, hazy and even slightly dreamlike in places, with a stronger pop sensibility, while still never completely losing that rock touch underneath it.

That whole progression is part of what made In Chicago stand out to me so much. Because when I put that album on, I’m not sitting there thinking, “this is a rock album with some blues influence.” I’m hearing harmonica, piano, blues guitar phrasing, shuffles, those vocals, the entire feel of the record, and thinking, this is blues.

I think the underlying problem is that music databases often treat genre as several different things at once for examplee:

Artist identity. “Fleetwood Mac = rock band.”  
Commercial shelving. A record company needs somewhere broad to put the album.  
Historical classification. A band can end up grouped under Rock because that is where they eventually sit in the broader history of popular music.  
Album sound. What the actual record sounds like.  
Track level sound. Which can differ even within one album.

But those are not the same thing and i still do not understand why i'm listening to an R&B album and it's listed as Pop .

And that’s what I find interesting. Sometimes the genre seems to describe where an artist sits in music history more than what the specific recording in front of you actually sounds like.

Surely if albums are going to be given individual genres, the recording itself should be one of the biggest factors in deciding what that genre is.

As a longtime fan of both projects, I only just pondered on how similar the career trajectories of Swans and Godflesh have been.

Godflesh's latest album *Decay* was released yesterday, their 10th studio full-length and the 4th since their comeback in 2014 after a 13 year hiatus. What started as raw and angry sound that pioneered the industrial metal genre was later refined into an equally abrasive and heavy style but with more maturity and experimentation, combining elements from softer genres like shoegaze and electronica into their heavily down-tuned style. In tandem with this shift of direction, the themes in their lyrics, written mostly by founder/frontman Justin K Broadrick, went from corruption, nihilism, and hatred from the eyes of a young brit to a more introspective view on the world, inner self, and death, brought forth from one who experienced all hardships of life and the wisdom it provides.

Despite their differences in sound, the path of Michael Gira and his band Swans wasn't so different. Started back in the early 80s apart of the NYC No Wave scene, Swan's early works were just as abrasive, noisy, experimental and angry, with their first four albums being straight industrial noise rock before adding experimentations of other sounds into their sound. Their comeback album in 2010 *My Father Will Guide Me Up a Rope to the Sky* marked the end of a 14 year hiatus, and while not considered as remarkable compared to the other new-era albums like *The Seer* and *To Be Kind*, was still met with positive reception and excitement that their return was going to be long-term, eventually proving true. Their sound became noticeably more mature in style and concept, focusing on arrangement of a larger palette of instruments, motifs, and repetition with themes of spirituality anchoring the album's theme while maintaining a loud, powerful sound that would later be dubbed as the "Big Sound" era of Swans.

What once were two young entities dispelling their anger with society from different sides of the world, grew older and much wiser, reflecting on the hardships and experiences of life which reflected in their evolving sounds. It's not easy for bands to take a 10+ year long hiatus and come back with not only the same intensity but with an even greater following than the first half of their careers, but both projects achieved just that, furthering their influence and legacies as some of the best experimental projects to have ever been created.

While Broadrick has come out and announced this latest album will mark the beginning of the end for the project, it's hard to say whether or not Swans will also be winding down too due to Gira's age, but without any indication from the latter to be substantiated, both acts left an incredible footprint on music as a whole for generations to come.

Were the mid to late 60s and early 70s one of the golden ages of pop music?

The 1960s and 1970s were an unbeatable peak for popular music. To me, the late 60s hit this absolute sweet spot where people had moved past the overly sterilized crooner 20s-40s ballroom music and the overly pretentious but held back 50s rock rebellion marked by people like Elvis and Little Richard, but at the same tome we hadn't yet hit at over-commericalized 80s pop dominate that started with MTV with people like Madonna that is still pretty much the dominant style today.

Motown and The Supremes, The Beatles, The Doors, The Kinks, and The Mamas and the Papas, Jimi Hendrix emerged during this stretch in the 60s as well, and it continued on as in the 70s you had Marvin Gaye, Bowie and The Bee Gees, so I think it all just came together at the perfect moment.

This is also why around the time the Wall of Sound technique was becoming incredibly popular. Studio tech had developed just enough by then that the recordings don't sound nearly as dated anything pre 1965 but still doesn’t have that artificial music video sound that became prominent in the early 80s and stayed mainstream until maybe the 2000s.

Why do "hometown" songs hit so different when you actually know the place?

I grew up in a small industrial town nobody's ever heard of, and for years the only music that felt like "home" to me was generic nostalgia stuff that could've been about anywhere. Then a few years back I found a local band that wrote a song literally about the river and the factory smell and the one intersection everyone complains about, and it wrecked me in a way no Springsteen or Mellencamp song ever could, even though those guys are clearly more talented. It made me think about how weirdly specific music has to get before it stops being "relatable" in the vague sense and starts being personal in the real sense. Like there's universal nostalgia (small towns, growing up, leaving home) that a lot of people connect with, and then there's this other thing that only works if you've actually stood on that specific street corner.   
Does anyone else have a song like this, something too niche or too local to ever chart, that hits harder than any "objectively better" song about the same general feeling?

Is there a specific musical instrument you associate with a particular mood or feeling question?

I've been thinking about this a lot lately. Sometimes when I hear a specific instrument it just immediately conjures up a certain vibe. Like a specific feeling or even a memory. 

  
For me the cello always makes me feel melancholic or thoughtful. It has such a rich deep sound. It's beautiful but always a little sad. If I hear a cello solo I instantly feel a certain way. 

  
Then there's the electric guitar for excitement or rebellion. Especially a distorted one. It just gets my blood pumping. It's the sound of rock and roll and always feels high energy.

  
Flutes or harps often feel ethereal or magical to me. They have this light airy quality that just transports me. It's like fairy music.

  
Is it just me or do others experience this too? Are there instruments that just hit you in a particular way every time you hear them? What are your associations?

Molly Hatchet is kind of fun.

For decades I've seen Molly Hatchet albums at second-hand stores and never, not even once, was curious about what they sounded like. I assumed cheesy metal because of the Viking looking mascot. But out of curiosity's sake I put it on my streamer and realized this is the band that did the song Flirtin' With Disaster. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OgNAfSENE68&list=RDOgNAfSENE68&start\_radio=1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OgNAfSENE68&list=RDOgNAfSENE68&start_radio=1)  

  
As someone that grew up in a place with ZERO rock on the radio (country, tejano and a top 40 station that included hits in Spanish). I learned about classic rock later in life and just assumed that maybe that was a Charlie Daniels Band song. I was exposed to MTV rock, but classic rock? Nope. It was so bad I would tape rock stations when I went out of town just to hear something different. 

If you like southern, twangy, over the top bluesy rock that whole album is amazing. The song Fall of the Peacekeepers is pretty amazing as well from a different albumhttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BjeY2EbokSA&list=RDBjeY2EbokSA&start\_radio=1. 

  
It turns out that at least that whole Flirtin' with Disaster album is a good time. Overly technical southern rock with more freewheeling solos than necessary. You get a feeling, especially because they're from Florida, some of these guys would be in technical death metal bands today due to how complex the guitar game is. It's fun. It's party music for the most part. 

Also, this band is a total mess when it comes to who is even in the band and what they were up to. They are touring right now and no original members are still alive. Total Madness. I don't know if they've had more lineup changes than Napalm Death or TSOL. There's absolutely no reason for a wiki page to be this long https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly\_Hatchet. 

I kind of wish Danny McBride would star in a movie about these guys. They started off as a cover band that would just play every club in Jacksonville and then change the band name and do it all over again. They also sounded so much like Lynyrd Skynyrd that a member of LS was on the verge of heading into the studio with them when the plane crash happened. 

Anyway, just wanted to post something fun and talk about a bunch of crazy southern guys making music that anyone born below the Mason Dixon line will be naturally drawn to. Something about that twangy sound that will get to you if your from the South, makes me think of Bret Hinds and his bluegrass pickin' solos on all those Mastodon albums. I bet 100% my uncles were smoking bowls to this in their younger days.

Where do chillout and lounge people hang out these days (on the web)?

I have been diving deep into this space lately, both listening and making my own stuff, and I am curious where the community actually lives online. Reddit has a few scattered subs like r/downtempo and r/listentothis, but activity feels thin compared to other genres.

Artists like Fragile State and Tosca defined a lot of what this genre sounds like for me, but I rarely see them discussed anywhere outside the occasional YouTube comment section. Are there active forums, or blogs still going for this kind of music, or has it mostly moved to algorithmic playlists with no real community attached?

Curious what people who have been into this longer than me have found, as I am eager to connect with possible listeners and get to know other people in this niche.

Ella Langley's Choosin Texas - Why Has This Song Had Absolutely No Drop-Off from the charts?

When it first reached that ranking, I assumed it was mostly because of the “new song” appeal. It was everywhere on social media, getting used in videos, played in stores, on the radio, etc., so I could understand why it would shoot up the charts initially.

But now it’s been sitting up there for a good 22 consecutive weeks and it literally hasn’t budged. At this point, after hearing it for what feels like the 30 millionth time on the radio, I genuinely don’t understand what is keeping it there. You’d think the novelty would have worn off by now, especially with how much it’s been played and how long it’s been out.

I’m not even saying it’s a bad song, because obviously there’s clearly something about it that people like. I just don’t understand how it has managed to maintain that level of popularity for this long without any real drop-off. What am I missing? Is it still genuinely resonating with people that much, or is there something else keeping it so high on the charts?

What's the best way to pay for music these days?

I would like to pay artists for their music, but unfortunately with the way things are set-up now it's a little difficult to figure out the best way.

Obviously streaming is easiest. Tons of options, available wherever you go via your phone, etc. But you pay for the service, not directly to the artist.

Physical media (CDs, Vinyl) is an option, but only if you have a CD player or record player, and you're not going to lug those around with you.

You can pay for music on iTunes, but putting those digital songs on your phone takes up a ton of storage, not sure if there's a workaround for that.

So, is it buying the album on Bandcamp just so money goes directly to the artist, and continuing to stream? Buying merch from the artist?  Thoughts?

Almost all of the good indie pop and rock musicians these days are fronted by female vocalists. Why is that? Or is it just me?

I have been listening to punk, indie, alternative pop and rock for about 40 years now. There have always been some female vocalists, but they were in the minority. I can’t say that I have gone out of my way to listen to female vocalists, but have nothing against them. 

These days almost all of the indie artists I find myself listening to are women: Waxahatchee, Adrienne Lenker, Snail Mail, Japanese Breakfast, Soccer Mommy, Courtney Barnett, Hurrah for the Riff Raff, The Beths, and so many more. 

Is there really just an explosion of fantastic female artists, or a dearth of guys in indie pop/rock, or am I just in some kind of bubble?

Haircut One Hundred: are they more than "Love Plus One"?

Note: Brought over from / r/ HaircutOneHundred. A slightly longer Haircut 100 post than I intended - but I've been listening to Pelican West again, and I have thoughts, and want yours.

As the mod there, and to the surprise of absolutely no one, I've been thinking a lot about Haircut One Hundred lately. They seem to have been assigned a very specific little slot in 1980s history: silly name, North of England meets Nantucket clothes, attractive singer, horns, "Love Plus One," end of story.

That is not an entirely unfair take. They were young, stylish, and visibly having a good time in an era when a lot of bands were trying to look mysterious, brooding, or dangerous. Their name does sound like something made up at the last minute as a silly inside joke - and it was. When people do remember them, it is usually through "Love Plus One," maybe "Fantastic Day," and a general sense of early-'80s color and cheerfulness.

But I think Haircut 100 get written off because people confuse "happy pop" with empty pop. Their 1982 debut, Pelican West, is one of my favorite albums from that whole period. It is packed with good musicianship, strange little lyrical images, catchy tunes, and a layered sound that pulls from funk, jazz-pop, Afro-Caribbean percussion, and British guitar pop. It still feels like nobody else's.

Haircut 100 were not a standard guitar band with a saxophone player added for the single. The sax, percussion, bass, and drums are central to what makes the band work. They play like a real unit, not like a group built around Nick Heyward with a few fashionable touches added afterward.

Listen to "Favourite Shirts (Boy Meets Girl)" and the first thing you notice is that it moves. The bass does not just sit underneath the song; it takes its own winding route through the arrangement. The guitar is clipped and nervous. The percussion keeps things light on their feet, almost grinding, like a packed dancehall on a humid night. Then the horns come in - like someone pressed a Brasil '66 horn line into performing at sword-point - and make the whole thing feel even more alive.

It is a very poppy song, obviously, but not simple-minded pop. You can (try to!) put it on in the background and enjoy the tune - maybe without tapping your feet or dancing, this time - or you can focus on the rhythm section and hear how much work the band is doing. I wish Haircut 100 were talked about more as musicians, and not just as an image from old Top of the Pops clips.

"Love Plus One" is the big one, and I think it is much stranger than it first appears, or than people give it credit for.

The hook is so immediate that it can distract from the lyric: "I, I went off to the right / Without saying good goodbye / Where does it go from here? / Is it down to the lake I fear?" This is not a normal beginning-middle-end love story. It sounds like a half-remembered scene, full of travel, uncertainty, and somebody trying to make contact: "Ring, ring, ring, ring."

Nick Heyward later explained that the song started as "I went off to the Rhine," based on memories connected to his Swiss-German mother, family trips to Germany, lakes and forests, and "ring Anna" - calling home to his mother. The final lyric became "I went off to the right," but that dreamlike, memory-based quality remains.

That does not solve every line - not getting too Freud on you, but sometimes "a lyric is just a lyric" - and I would not want it to. The song feels personal without explaining itself. It is bright, for sure, but "Where does it go from here?" gives it a small thread of uncertainty. The song never offers a clean answer. It just keeps moving.

"Fantastic Day" is more direct. Its title tells you flat-out what it is going for, and the band gives it everything: bright horns, a bouncy rhythm, and a chorus that makes "fantastic" sound like something you can almost talk yourself into believing.

I have seen it dismissed as lightweight, which seems unfair. There is real skill in making a song this busy and polished sound effortless. Pop does not need to be sad or bleak to have substance, and few songs from 1982 make three minutes of joy sound this convincing.

The less popular cuts are where Pelican West becomes more than an album built around three singles. "Lemon Firebrigade" is one of the best things on it. I like the title, obviously, but I also like how the song feels a little more tense and off-balance than the hits. The usual Haircut 100 ingredients are still here: busy Latin-infused bass, rattling percussion, horns that seem to have arrived overdressed, and guitar that never quite settles into a standard rock shape.

"Marine Boy," "Snow Girl," and "Milk Film" keep up the album's fondness for characters and images that feel like they came from postcards, cartoons, or childhood memories. "Kingsize (You're My Little Steam Whistle)" is exactly as ridiculous - and enjoyable - as it sounds. The record has a lot of whimsy, no question, but I do not think whimsy is automatically a bad thing. Well-played whimsy will cover a multitude of sins.

"Calling Captain Autumn" is probably the track I would play for somebody who thinks Haircut 100 were all sugar and horns. It is still recognizably them, but it has a more reflective feel. The title sounds like it could be from a children's show, but the music has a real late-summer sadness to it. At least, that is how it lands for me.

And then there is "Boat Party," closely tied to this era of the band even though it was not on the original UK Pelican West track list. It is looser and longer than the big singles, and gives the players room to settle into the rhythm. It is a useful one to play for anyone who thinks Haircut 100 were just a set of neat pop singles.

The frustrating part of the Haircut 100 story is how brief this lineup's run was. Pelican West came out in February 1982, reached No. 2 in the UK, and produced "Favourite Shirts," "Love Plus One," and "Fantastic Day." Nick Heyward left in early 1983; the remaining members carried on with 1984's Paint and Paint, with Marc Fox on lead vocals. It is worth hearing, but it is not Pelican West part two.

People sometimes call Haircut 100 a one-album band, and in a narrow sense, I understand why. But that phrase can sound like a put-down. If you make one album that is as lively, distinctive, and replayable as Pelican West, then you have done something plenty of much longer-running bands never manage.

Yes, it sounds very much like 1982. The horns, the clothes, the hair, the production, the cheerful confidence: it is all there. I don't see that as a problem. Sometimes I want an old record to sound old. I want the horns, the strange confidence, and the sense that 1982 briefly believed pop music could be this colorful.

Pelican West sounds like six young musicians deciding that pop music could be clever, danceable, a little weird, and completely unafraid of color. They were right.

My pick for the best Haircut 100 non-single is probably "Lemon Firebrigade," though "Calling Captain Autumn" and "Boat Party" would be close behind. What is yours? And which other bands get dismissed as "lightweight" mainly because they made joy sound easy?

Where does Karen O fit in the female rocker pantheon?

The Yeah Yeah Yeahs are a pretty well respected band but I don’t hear a lot of talk about them, though the documentary Meet Me in the Bathroom and the New York indie scene was a pretty good capture of them. But I remember seeing the YYYs playing on Letterman (“Date with the Night”) and audience completely shocked and her just laughing at the end of the song. 

Fever to Tell, Show Your Bones and It’s Blitz! show a real progression from in your face post punk to a more melodic and even danceable sound. Mosquito was a misstep but Cool It Down returns to the fold of great records and she did some notable work on Where the Wild Things Are  soundtrack. 

Everyone knows “Maps” but better representations are “Man,” “Y Control”, “Isis,”  “Down Boy,” Fancy” and “Dragon Queen.”  I’ve heard Karen O be compared to PJ Harvey but I think if her as a little closer to Chrissie Hynde or Siouxsie but perhaps more heart and warmer (well, Chrissie has that too in a different way). I don’t think anyone does a rock shriek or yelp quite like Karen O and also manage to maintain some popular music sensibilities. 

Does she fit in there with those other female greats?  I sorta feel like she came along later so maybe isn’t discussed in that group but belongs there in spirit. I feel like there’s a gap in this period that people forget - who else around this time was carrying the torch?
